courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Alpha compositing sorted splats at one pixel
md: Pixel color is a weighted sum of splat colors with weights $\alpha_i T_i$. Order changes who gets the weight, and every splat with nonzero weight receives a gradient.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
md: Choose by failure mode. Tagged pointers: cheap, but need wide CAS or spare bits and type-stable nodes. LL/SC: ABA-free in principle, rarely usable directly. Hazard pointers: bounded garbage under stalls, cost per access. Epochs: cheapest per access, but one stalled thread blocks all reclamation.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Who are you, and what may you do: authentication vs authorization
md: Being logged in is not a permission. Authentication tells the server *who* is asking; it says nothing about *which* objects and functions that person may touch. Each request needs both answers.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Cases: USPS, Peloton and Optus, APIs that trusted too much
md: Adding a login in front of an endpoint is not the fix for broken authorization. Peloton's partial fix and USPS's whole design show the result: every registered user, and anyone can register, gets everyone's data.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM relay: forwarding someone else's login, and how signing stops it
md: Relay borrows a live NTLM sign-in instead of stealing a hash. It is stopped by binding authentication to the session or channel: SMB signing, LDAP signing and channel binding, and EPA on HTTPS. Then remove the bait: LLMNR, NBT-NS and NTLM itself. To respond, isolate the rogue host, review what the relayed identity did on the target, and revoke any certificate issued through a relayed login.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: DCSync: asking a domain controller for every password
md: DCSync abuses a legitimate protocol: anyone with both replication rights can ask a DC for any password hash. Control who holds those rights, audit 4662 with the replication GUIDs, and treat a DCSync as compromise of every account.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Why documents and scripts: the chain an analyst unpicks
md: Every demo in this course uses harmless files built for it. Never fetch real samples onto a work machine: get them only through your organisation's incident process, keep them zipped with a password, and open them only in the isolated lab described in the malware course.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Unpacking II: dumping from memory, and payloads hidden in data
md: Carve, decode, confirm. Find where the code reads data, extract exactly those bytes, decode them step by step, and check each step against the code that does it. A decoding you guessed is a hypothesis until the code agrees.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Return-oriented programming as Shacham defined it
md: Misconception: "ROP needs special gadget functions, so removing dangerous library functions stops it." Shacham's thesis is the opposite: any large enough body of x86 code contains enough sequences, many of them unintended. The fix is checking control flow, not pruning code.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Command and control at the design level
md: Do not treat C2 detection as "find the red team's tool". CISA's federal red team (AA24-193A) "deployed over seven different implants" with different host and network signatures precisely to show that defenders who hunt one framework's fingerprints miss the rest. Detect the behaviour every implant shares: periodic contact, new destinations, odd egress from servers.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Reporting, retesting and where to practise
md: Measure a red or purple team by what it changes: findings with owners, fixes retested with the same procedure, and tests that keep running afterwards. Everything is done under written authorisation, inside agreed rules, with a way to stop in minutes.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
md: The model does not execute tools. It only emits a structured request. Whether a shell command actually runs, and with what permissions, is decided entirely by harness code, which is why safety controls belong in the harness.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The read path: scoring memories by recency, importance and relevance
md: Recency decay does not resolve conflicts. A stale fact with high importance and relevance still makes the cut, so the newer fact helps only if the reader happens to trust it more. Resolve contradictions on the write path; use scoring to choose among facts that are all still true.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: From a benchmark to an environment: reset, step and a checker
md: An agentic RL environment is a benchmark task turned into a loop you can run millions of times: `reset` to a clean sandbox, `step` per tool call, and a programmatic checker that produces the reward at the end. The simulated user in tau-bench is part of the environment, not part of the policy.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: A toy agent loop: watching a web page give orders
md: The dangerous line is never the model call. It is the loop that turns model output into actions. Put your controls there.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Model supply chain: pickle files, safetensors and signing
md: Loading a pickle is running code. Prefer safetensors, load PyTorch files with weights_only=True, and verify a signature or hash from a source you trust before loading anything.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Cheap surrogates for DFT: graph networks and interatomic potentials
md: Judge a discovery surrogate by what it does to DFT spending: precision (hit rate), recall, and DAF on unrelaxed inputs. A low regression error does not guarantee good decisions near the hull.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a green-list watermark and detector in 60 lines
md: The two p-values for the watermarked run differ by a factor of about 78,000 ($5.9 \times 10^{-30}$ versus $4.6 \times 10^{-25}$). Both are tiny here, but the same gap at a borderline score decides whether someone is accused. Three Bricks reports exact tests because the normal tail is too optimistic exactly where thresholds sit, deep in the tail.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Capturing calls: glibc mtrace and LD_PRELOAD interposers
md: What interposition misses: statically linked programs (LD_PRELOAD is a feature of the dynamic linker), secure-execution binaries such as set-user-ID programs (the linker ignores LD_PRELOAD paths with slashes), and any memory that bypasses malloc: direct mmap, custom arenas and pools, GPU allocations. heaptrack's README notes pool allocators need code annotations to be profiled.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
md: LOF answers a different question from Isolation Forest: not how isolated a point is, but how isolated it is relative to its own neighborhood. Use it when normal data has regions of very different density; pay for it with k-nearest-neighbor searches and a k to tune.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023), item by item
md: Most of the API Top 10 is not exotic. It is a missing check (who owns this, who may call this, how many times), a forgotten endpoint, or misplaced trust in another system.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OpenID Connect: logging users in with an ID token
md: ID token: for the client, proves a login happened (check aud = your client_id and nonce). Access token: for the API, grants access (the API checks aud = itself). Never accept one where the other is expected.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to API and token attacks
md: Tokens move the security perimeter into data: who issued it, with which key, for which audience, for how long. Log those fields on every request, alert on the impossible ones, and rehearse revoking at scale.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Writing rules: Semgrep and CodeQL on the same code
md: Write a custom rule when a bug teaches you a pattern: after every incident or review finding, ask "where else does this pattern appear?" and encode it. That is variant analysis, and it turns one fix into a class fix.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: SSVC: decisions instead of scores
md: SSVC turns "how bad is it?" into "what do we do, and how fast?". The inputs that matter most are exploitation status and your own context: exposure and how essential the system is. A score cannot know the second.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
md: ARIES in one line: **repeat history, then undo the losers, logging every undo as a redo-only CLR whose UndoNextLSN skips what is already undone**. That makes recovery **idempotent**, meaning that running it again after a partial run ends in the same state as running it once: crash during analysis or redo and you simply start over; crash during undo and you resume where the CLRs say.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast
md: `gather` does not cancel siblings on failure. With the default `return_exceptions=False`, the first exception propagates to the caller but the docs state the other awaitables "won't be cancelled and will continue to run". If you want per-item errors without losing the batch, pass `return_exceptions=True` and inspect each result; if one failure should stop everything, use a `TaskGroup`.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Cooperative scheduling: blocking, budgets and cancellation
md: The budget only helps tasks that keep awaiting **Tokio** resources. It cannot interrupt a tight CPU loop or a blocking call, and the Tokio team has said it will not detect blocked workers and add threads automatically. Fixing those is your job.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
md: A pretrained audio model never sees a whole clip at once. It sees fixed 0.96 s log-mel patches and returns one embedding and one score vector per patch. Everything about clip-level decisions (lesson 3) is about combining those per-patch outputs.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: How offline cracking works: guesses, lists, rules and arithmetic
md: Offline cracking = guess, hash, compare, at the attacker's full hardware speed. Defenders control two things: how many guesses a password needs (length, unpredictability, blocklists) and how expensive each guess is (a slow, salted hash).

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Wearing MFA down: SIM swaps, push fatigue and Uber 2022
md: MFA is only as strong as its weakest step. SMS inherits the phone network's weaknesses; plain push inherits human fatigue. Number matching helps against fatigue; phishing-resistant MFA removes the whole class.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: End-to-end science agents: AI Scientist and co-scientist
md: End-to-end science agents fail at the steps where nothing external checks them: invented numbers, unfair comparisons, edits to their own limits. Put independent checks (sandboxes, reproducibility, human experts) at exactly those points.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: x86-64 on Linux and macOS: the System V calling convention
md: Do not apply Windows habits to Linux binaries. On Windows the first argument is in `rcx`; on Linux and macOS `rcx` is the fourth. Misreading the convention shifts every argument by several positions and makes a correct analysis look nonsensical. Check the file format first: PE means Microsoft x64, ELF or Mach-O on x86-64 means System V.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Ternary weights: log2(3), absmean and the power of zero
md: "1-bit LLM" is the family name, not the bit count. BitNet b1.58 weights are ternary (about 1.58 bits), the original BitNet was binary (1 bit), and in both the activations are 8-bit and the embeddings stay in higher precision.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: train a tiny BitNet and run it from packed bytes
md: The whole method fits on a laptop: a quantizer in the forward pass, an STE in the backward pass, then 2 bits per weight and integer adds at inference. The hard part in practice is the kernel, and matching training's quantizers exactly.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: A browser runs hostile code all day: the threat model
md: Misconception: "a sandbox escape is worse than a renderer bug, so it must be Critical." Chromium rates a renderer sandbox escape **High** because it needs the precondition of a compromised renderer. Critical is reserved for bugs that reach privileged code straight from a web page, or full chains.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Memory safety strategy: the Rule of 2, MiraclePtr, Rust and RLBox
md: Misconception: "a sandbox makes a memory bug harmless." It makes it worth less. A sandboxed decoder bug still gives code execution inside that sandbox, which is why Chromium still fixes and rewards such bugs as High, and why the Rule of 2 prefers removing the unsafe language when it can.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Compaction: merging sorted runs and organizing levels
md: Compaction converts a growing pile of overlapping files into a few large sorted runs. It is what keeps LSM reads and space bounded, and it is paid for with extra writes: every byte is rewritten each time it moves down a level.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: LRU-K: evict by the K-th most recent reference
md: LRU-K is not "keep the last K timestamps and you are done". Without a correlated reference period, a transaction that touches a page twice in a millisecond makes it look hot; without retained history, every page re-entering the pool starts at infinite distance and is evicted first.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Availability engineering: nines, redundancy and failure domains
md: Availability = uptime over total time. Hard dependencies multiply availabilities; independent redundant copies multiply failure rates; MTTR is a lever as strong as MTBF. Redundancy is only as good as its independence, so map failure domains, including software versions and admin identities.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups attackers cannot reach: immutability and isolated recovery
md: Assume production identity is lost. Give backups their own control plane, immutable and time-based retention, delayed and out-of-band-approved deletions, keys you cannot lose, alerts on every significant change, and restore into an isolated environment before anything returns to production.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Regulated resilience: DORA testing, TLPT and UK impact tolerances
md: DORA requires a BIA, backup and restore procedures with segregated restore systems, yearly continuity and switchover tests, a crisis function, and TLPT on production every three years for designated firms. The UK sets impact tolerances per important business service and requires proof, by severe but plausible scenario tests, that firms stay within them.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Generating with patches: the BLT decoding loop and its real cost
md: In BLT generation the latent model runs only when a patch closes, but the entropy model, encoder and decoder run on every byte in sequence. Fewer FLOPs per byte and lower latency are different goals; fixed patches, caches and speculative drafting are the levers for the second.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Data races: pthreads in C versus Send and Sync in Rust
md: Data race: unsynchronized conflicting accesses, undefined behavior, ruled out at compile time by the borrow rules plus Send and Sync. Race condition: a timing-dependent logic bug, still possible, still memory safe.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Why one load can cost 3 cycles or 240
md: Latency numbers are not constants of nature. Drepper's are for a Pentium M, CMU's for Haswell, and every CPU differs. Use them to reason about *ratios* (a DRAM access costs tens to hundreds of L1 hits), and measure your own machine before quoting absolute cycles.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Activation patching worked through: two directions and a shortcut
md: Denoising asks whether a component is enough to restore the behavior; noising asks whether the behavior needs it. AND-like circuits hide from denoising, OR-like backups hide from noising, and gradient shortcuts are trustworthy only for small patches.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Limitations, and tracing circuits yourself
md: An attribution graph explains one prompt in one replacement model. It is not proof of a general algorithm, it is silent about attention's choices, and any path through error nodes is unexplained. State those limits whenever you report a circuit.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
md: Pick the propensity source by how much user disruption you can afford: randomization or swaps are simplest and most trustworthy, EM and intervention harvesting use existing logs but rest on model assumptions, and DLA learns everything jointly. Every option inherits the click model's assumptions; if users behave like a cascade, a position-only propensity is misspecified.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Browser extensions: someone else's code in every page
md: Nothing on facebook.com was vulnerable in that case. An extension with access to a site is effectively a trusted script on that site. For a site owner this risk sits outside your perimeter; for an organisation that manages its employees' browsers, it is squarely inside it.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Where the evidence lives when there is no server to seize
md: Cloud incident response reconstructs what identities did through the provider's API, across four evidence layers: control plane, data plane, workload and identity provider. What you can prove is decided before the incident, by which logs were on and where they were kept.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Identity incidents: tokens, consent grants and mailbox rules
md: Misconception: "we reset the password, so the attacker is out". A reset leaves forwarding rules, registered MFA methods, OAuth consent grants and app passwords in place, and already issued access tokens keep working for up to about an hour in apps without CAE. Disable, revoke, then hunt for each kind of persistence.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: The same guardrails in Azure Policy and Google organization policy
md: Identity rules (RBAC, IAM) say who may act. Configuration guardrails (Azure Policy, Google organization policy, AWS SCPs used as preventive controls) say what no one may build, such as storage that accepts account keys or service accounts with downloadable keys. Set them high in the hierarchy, start in audit mode, then deny.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: The shared responsibility model, and when the provider gets it wrong
md: Common misconception: "we are on a big cloud, so the provider handles security." The provider secures its platform. Your identities, keys, data and configuration are yours, and even provider-side bugs usually ended with a customer to-do: regenerate keys after ChaosDB, update agents after OMIGOD.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Logging and detection: what key abuse looks like in CloudTrail
md: Log everything that changes configuration, keep it in a place attackers cannot reach, turn on data events for buckets that hold sensitive data, and alert on a short list of high-signal events: logging disabled, root use, new access keys and users, policy changes, and known credentials used from new places.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
md: Three things the silhouette cannot do. It is undefined for k = 1, so it can never tell you "this data has no clusters" (our k = 3 winner at 0.54 is not strong evidence of anything). It needs all pairwise distances, so it costs O(n squared) work. And it rewards compact well-separated blobs, so it is biased toward the kind of answer k-means produces, which makes it a poor referee between k-means and a density method.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets
md: A column in memory is a few flat buffers: values (or offsets plus data) and a validity bitmap. Flat, typed, contiguous buffers are what make tight loops and SIMD over columns possible.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Misconception: the `inline` keyword forces inlining. It is a hint plus linkage rules: rules about how the function's definition is shared between files. At -O2 the compiler inlines functions you never marked, and may refuse ones you did. At -O0 GCC inlines nothing unless the function has `__attribute__((always_inline))`.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: -ffast-math assumes no NaNs or infinities (-ffinite-math-only), so code that relies on IEEE behavior of NaNs and infinities can give incorrect results. Clang has deprecated -Ofast because an optimization flag changing the observable behavior of correct code surprises people. Enable fast-math per file or per function when you have verified the numerics, not globally.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
md: Misconception: a system prompt saying "ignore instructions on web pages" solves injection. It helps, but the model reads that prompt and the attacker's text through the same channel. Defenses that do not depend on the model obeying (no secrets in the VM, network allowlists, harness-enforced confirmations) are what hold when the model is fooled.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
md: TSan must see **all** synchronization. Code not built with the flag (a prebuilt library, inline assembly) can cause false positives or missed races. That is why Rust's std should be rebuilt with the sanitizer via `-Zbuild-std`. The Rust unstable book also says Rust TSan does not support `std::sync::atomic::fence` or synchronization done in inline assembly, and rebuilding std does not change that.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Weaker but useful: sequential and causal consistency
md: Herlihy and Wing showed sequential consistency is **not local**: every object can be sequentially consistent while the system as a whole is not. Linearizability is local, which is one reason it composes better.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Must-haves and nice-to-haves need different machinery
md: Hard constraints decide **who is in**; soft constraints decide **the order**. Never let a preference buy its way past a requirement, and never let a preference silently remove someone.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: SAT solvers: DPLL, unit propagation and clause learning
md: CDCL = DPLL + conflict analysis that learns a clause + backjumping to the level where the learned clause becomes unit and forces (asserts) its last literal + watched literals for cheap propagation + activity-based decisions and restarts. Each conflict teaches the solver something it never has to rediscover.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pinning by digest, signing images and verifying at admission
md: Pin by digest so you always run the same bytes; sign in CI and verify at admission so you only run bytes your pipeline produced.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
md: A pod's identity is its service account token plus whatever cloud role it can reach. Mount tokens only where needed, give each app its own service account, and map cloud access per service account instead of per node.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Escapes in the runtime: runc CVE-2019-5736 and Leaky Vessels
md: Runtime escapes come from the runtime briefly holding host resources while entering a container. Patch the runtime everywhere, run only trusted images, and use user namespaces so that even a successful escape lands as an unprivileged user.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
md: Deletes and resets are rare in training data and rare in casual testing, so they are the operations most likely to be broken in your system. Test them on purpose: write cases for *drop X*, *any X is fine*, *never mind the Y* and *start over*.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Storing state server-side and measuring it
md: Store the state server-side with a version and an event log; evaluate it with joint goal accuracy and per-operation recall, not just slot accuracy or end-to-end clicks.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Unfaithful without a hint: rationalization on natural prompts
md: Reversed question pairs detect unfaithfulness without planting anything: a consistent reasoner cannot answer Yes to both. This is behavioral evidence, necessary but not sufficient for faithful internal computation, and it shows frontier models rationalize rarely but measurably.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Streams, the default stream trap, and events
md: Three independent facts, often confused. A stream gives you **ordering** (and is always sequential inside itself). Separate streams give you **permission** to overlap. The hardware (`asyncEngineCount`, concurrent kernel support, free SMs) decides whether overlap actually **happens**. Two streams on a one-copy-engine GPU will still serialize their two transfers against each other.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Training a reranker: pointwise, pairwise, listwise and hard negatives
md: Hard negative mining has a trap: MS MARCO labels about one relevant passage per query, so many top-ranked unlabeled passages are actually relevant. Training to push them down teaches the model wrong lessons. mine_hard_negatives offers margins and a max_score cap partly to skip such false negatives.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: When hashes break: MD5, Flame and the SHA-1 collision
md: "It is only a checksum" is how MD5 and SHA-1 linger. Any place where an attacker can choose the input that gets hashed (certificates, signed documents, deduplication, commit ids, package lockfiles) needs collision resistance.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Padding oracles: when an error message decrypts your data
md: A padding oracle needs two things: decryption of unauthenticated ciphertext, and any observable difference (message, status code, timing, log line, connection reset) between padding failures and other failures. Remove the first and the second cannot matter: authenticate before you decrypt.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Never trust parameters: invalid curves, blank signatures, pinning
md: "The library checks that" is a claim to test, not assume. Java's verifier was a mainstream library. Run published test vectors such as Project Wycheproof against the exact library versions you ship.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
md: Atoms are hardware facts, TiledMMA and TiledCopy are spatial arrangements of atoms, and partition_A/B/C or partition_S/D (source and destination) turn a tile into per-thread fragments. Swapping the atom (FMA, mma.sync, wgmma) changes the instruction without rewriting the loops.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
md: Do not assume every CXL device behaves like Pond's model. Sun et al. measured three real devices: one had load latency only 35% longer than a remote-socket DDR5 node, while the other two were about 2x and 3x longer. Their bandwidth efficiency also differed widely by controller. Emulating CXL with a remote NUMA socket, as early research did, can mislead in both directions.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Van Buren (2021): gates up or down, not good or bad motives
md: Van Buren is not a licence. Misusing data you may open can still be fraud, a privacy violation, a breach of contract, a firing offence or a state crime (lesson 4). And it says nothing about getting past a gate that is down: guessing a password or exploiting a bug to reach an area is still the off-limits kind.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Writing and selling tools: Marcus Hutchins and dual-use code
md: Writing security tools is legal almost everywhere. Laws target tools designed primarily for crime and people who supply them intending, or believing likely, criminal use. Context is evidence: who you sell to, how you advertise, what the features are for.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Evidence in court: authenticity, hearsay and chain of custody
md: Courts ask: is it what you say it is (authenticity), was it made routinely at the time (business records), and who could have changed it (chain of custody)? Automatic logs, hashes at collection and a tamper-evident custody record answer all three.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
md: Using 280M-proxy weights for an 8B model is an empirical bet that good weights transfer across a 30x jump in scale. It paid off here, but the paper lists why weights transfer, and how far, as open questions, and its 1B proxy produced a worse 8B model than the 280M one (lesson 6). Weights also assume a token budget: lesson 5 shows what happens when you reuse them for a longer run.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
md: Clean before you mix. Cheap rules remove describable junk, a perplexity filter keeps text resembling a reference (with its biases), and exact plus near deduplication removes copies. Each step shrinks domains, so redo the epoch math of lesson 5 and rerun the mixing step on the cleaned data.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Choosing a layout: hot/cold splits, ECS chunks and columnar data
md: List the hot loops, write down which fields each one touches and whether it streams or jumps, then pick the layout that packs those bytes together. Re-measure when the access pattern changes.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Tokens and masks: taking real values out of systems
md: Dynamic masking changes what is displayed, not what can be queried. Against anyone who can write their own WHERE clauses it is not a security boundary; use column permissions (lesson 8), tokens or encryption there.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a data security programme, and practice
md: Data security is a loop: find, label, keep less, protect, watch, destroy, with each finding feeding back into the inventory. Measure each stage, and judge controls by who can still cause the data to be read.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honey records and honeywords: decoys inside your data
md: Our toy honeywords are small edits of the real password, which a smart attacker can often see through. The paper spends much of its length on generating decoys that are as likely as real user choices ("flatness"). Weak generation lets an attacker pick the real password far more often than 1 in $k$.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce
md: DST makes a run a pure function of (code, seed). Faults can then be as aggressive and random as you like, because any failure they provoke can be replayed exactly by re-running one seed.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: CircleCI 2023: when the platform holding your secrets is breached
md: Encryption at rest did not save the secrets, because a running service must decrypt them to use them, and the attacker read the keys from a running process. The only secret a breached CI vendor cannot leak is one it never stored.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest
md: A sampling step is: one forward pass over the whole sequence, a guess at every masked slot, then keep the k most confident guesses and remask the rest. The schedule fixes k per step; the confidence ranking decides the order.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
md: Prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT; decode is memory-bound and sets TPOT. Putting both in one batch makes each phase pay for the other.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: From sectors to partitions to image files
md: Do not stop at the partitions. NIST SP 800-86 counts *free space* (areas not allocated to any partition, including whole deleted volumes) as a place where data may remain. Our lab disk already has 2,047 sectors before the first partition that no file system owns.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics from the defender's side: what each trick leaves
md: The cleanup is evidence too. A 1102 event, a reset journal or deleted shadow copies at 14:35 tell you someone with administrator rights was covering tracks then, which often dates the intrusion better than anything they deleted.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO is not "RLHF without a reward". It fits the same Bradley-Terry reward model, just parameterized through the policy. It also inherits the KL objective's $\beta$. What it removes is the separate reward network and on-policy sampling during training.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
md: Until phase 4, at least one store is complete and current, and the other one is being kept in step with it. That is what makes every earlier step reversible. Plan each phase so it can be rolled out gradually (by percentage of objects or code paths) and rolled back with a flag.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
md: Move one thing at a time, keep one store complete until the very end, and measure agreement continuously. The deletion in phase 4 is the only step that should be hard to undo.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale
md: Misconception: int8 means the model can only represent values between -128 and 127. The integers are codes; the scale maps them to any real range. What int8 limits is the number of distinct levels (256) inside that range, so the range you pick matters more than the bit width alone.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Ivanti Connect Secure, 2024: chained zero-days and a fooled checker
md: A clean integrity check is evidence, not proof. If an attacker reached root, the checker ran on a system the attacker controls. Trust measurements taken from outside the device, and rebuild when root was possible.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
md: Efficient reasoning asks a different question from test-time scaling. Not 'does more thinking help?' but 'how few thinking tokens reach the same accuracy on this particular problem?'

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Underthinking and early exit: stopping at the right moment
md: Long output does not tell you which failure you have. Overthinking re-solves an easy problem that was already right; underthinking abandons a promising approach on a hard one. The fixes differ: stop earlier in the first case, stay longer on each idea in the second.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Many spellings of one value: UTF-8 overlongs and base64 slack
md: Do not "fix" malformed input by cleaning it up and carrying on. Repairing an overlong sequence or dropping junk characters creates exactly the second spelling an attacker needs. Strict decoders that raise an error give every component the same answer: invalid.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Internationalised domain names, Punycode and what browsers show
md: Chromium's page is blunt that this is not a complete defence: it calls homographs "a limitation of how URLs are displayed in browsers in general" and lists other protections, such as Safe Browsing warnings and password managers that will not fill a password into a domain that is not exactly the right one. Treat the address bar as a hint, not a guarantee.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Where a sensor sits: kernel callbacks, minifilters and network filters
md: Misconception: "kernel mode makes a sensor untouchable." A kernel sensor can see everything, but so can any other code that reaches the kernel. An attacker who loads their own driver, or abuses a vulnerable signed one, is on equal footing with the sensor. That is exactly what the EDR-killer lesson covers.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Credential hardening: LAPS, LSA protection and Credential Guard
md: These controls each close one path: LAPS stops one local password from opening every machine; LSA protection stops ordinary processes reading LSASS; Credential Guard keeps the most reusable secrets out of LSASS's reach entirely; the ASR LSASS rule covers machines that can run neither. Check they are actually running, not just configured.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Scoring a disaggregation: MAE, NEP, NDE and F1
md: Metric details change numbers silently. The on/off threshold (10 W in NILMTK) sets F1; whether a paper reports NEP, NDE or energy accuracy changes which appliances look good; and per-appliance averages weight a lamp and a kettle equally while energy accuracy is dominated by the kettle. Always state the metric definition alongside a number.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
md: Blocking decides which pairs are compared, scoring decides which pairs are linked, and clustering decides which records share an ID. Tune the threshold on labeled data, because it trades false merges against missed merges.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Delegated vs application permissions, and who may consent
md: Misconception: an attacker needs an admin to consent before an app can steal mail. Delegated mail and file permissions are user-consentable by default, and the user's own mailbox is often the prize. Admin consent is needed for the tenant-wide versions, which is why attackers who compromise an admin go straight for application permissions.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Devices and the Primary Refresh Token: SSO bound to hardware
md: Misconception: a device-based Conditional Access rule means only company laptops get in. It means the token request came with a valid device identity. A device an attacker registers is a real device object, which is why device registration and join rights should be restricted and new registrations reviewed.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Taking over admins: help desks, MFA resets and rogue federation
md: Misconception: after a help-desk takeover, resetting the victim's password and MFA again evicts the attacker. If the attacker federated a domain or added an app credential, they can mint access without that account. Check federation settings, app credentials, role assignments and registered devices before calling it contained.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Closing a descriptor removes it from the interest list only when **every** descriptor referring to the same open file is closed. If a `dup` or a `fork` left another copy open, events can keep arriving for a number you already closed. Call `EPOLL_CTL_DEL` before closing when duplicates may exist.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
md: Resample queries, keep each query's pair of scores together, and report the interval along with the mean. A CI that crosses zero means your query set cannot tell the systems apart, whatever the point estimate says.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Why one leaked pointer defeats ASLR, and guessing at scale
md: ASLR is a secret, and like any secret it fails when leaked or when there are too few bits to stop guessing. Count the bits, avoid restart patterns that keep the secret constant, and treat information leaks as the first half of an exploit.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Fixing it: pad, align, or stop sharing writes
md: A fix needs both size and alignment: each hot item must start on a line boundary and be at least a line long. And pad only data that different threads write often; group everything else tightly.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Threats: what updates leak and how clients poison the model
md: Many local steps are not a privacy defense: in the Inverting Gradients experiments more local epochs did not make reconstruction harder. More examples per update did make it harder, but not safe. The paper's conclusion is that provable differential privacy is the only way to guarantee security.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Choosing gamma, falling back to pre-filter, and real results
md: ACORN is not free accuracy. The paper gives no connectivity guarantee for arbitrary data (neither does HNSW); connectivity is shown empirically. Very selective or strongly clustered predicates still need the pre-filter fallback, and ACORN-$\gamma$'s build is far slower than HNSW (SIFT1M 148.9 s vs 11.3 s, LAION-25M 38,007.5 s vs 1,147.2 s).

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Below the operating system: why boot code is the deepest foothold
md: Misconception: "I reinstalled the OS, so the machine is clean." A reinstall cleans the disk. It does not touch the SPI flash, and it may not touch every file on the boot partition.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Hardware roots of trust: Boot Guard, AMD PSB and Apple silicon
md: Hardware roots of trust are only as good as their configuration. Boot Guard and PSB both depend on the OEM fusing a key and choosing an enforcing policy; a board shipped unfused or with a measure-only policy gets little protection.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Using and measuring the kernels: benchmarks, numerics, decoding
md: Each generation chases the bottleneck the previous hardware exposed. FlashAttention removed HBM traffic for $S$ and $P$. FlashAttention-2 fixed work partitioning. FlashAttention-3 used Hopper's asynchrony to hide softmax and loads under the matmuls. FlashAttention-4 attacks the exponential unit and shared memory bandwidth, which stopped scaling with Blackwell's tensor cores.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Sampling with Euler steps: why curved paths need more steps
md: Sampling cost is set by how curved the learned paths are. A perfectly straight, constant-speed flow is solved exactly by one Euler step.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus: proving Rust functions with requires, ensures and invariants
md: Writing the invariant as `idx < n` looks natural but is wrong twice. Verus reports "invariant not satisfied before loop" (n can be 0) and "invariant not satisfied at end of loop body" (the last iteration makes idx == n).

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
md: The scale is a full-precision real number kept outside the FP8 data (in FP32), not a change to the format's exponent bias. The FP8 paper chose this deliberately: a software scale can take any value, while a programmable bias could only shift by powers of two.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust and safety: what these teams defend
md: Do not call it "just a business problem". Account takeover, scraping and carding cause data breaches and regulatory fines (you will see a EUR 265 million one in lesson 4), and the same signals and models also stop intrusions. Most fraud teams sit with, or next to, security.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Behaviour and velocity: counting what happens over time
md: Before a behavioural rule blocks anyone, test it against users of assistive technology and password managers. "Typed too fast" and "never moved the mouse" describe many legitimate users.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Card payments from zero: who is who, and where fraud lands
md: The issuer approves, the network sets the rules, and for card-not-present fraud the merchant usually pays when the cardholder disputes, unless the payment was strongly authenticated.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Measuring it: precision, recall, friction and the missing labels
md: Choose thresholds by total cost, not by precision or recall alone. Wait for labels to mature, and keep a small random holdout, because blocked events never tell you whether they were fraud.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: The write-ahead rule: flush the log first, pages later
md: The write-ahead rule, in PostgreSQL's words: changes to data files must be written only after the log records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage. A commit is durable once its commit record is flushed; data pages can be written much later.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Seeds, dictionaries and corpus minimisation
md: Seeds change results more than people expect. Klees et al. (lesson 9) found that AFLFast, an AFL variant that changes which corpus entries get the most fuzzing, produced over 1,000 crashing inputs on `nm` from an empty seed but only 24 from a small valid seed, statistically the same as AFL's 23. Always report which seeds you used.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Symbolic and concolic execution: solving for the input
md: Symbolic execution turns 'find an input that reaches here' into a math problem: collect the path condition, give it to an SMT solver, get a concrete input. Concolic execution keeps one foot in real execution to stay practical.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Jaro-Winkler, trigrams and token scorers on the same pairs
md: `partial_ratio` produces false positives on short strings: `fuzz.partial_ratio("ai", "said hello")` is 100 because `ai` appears inside `said`. Likewise `token_set_ratio` returns 100 for any subset, so `google` vs `google cloud platform team` is a perfect score. Use these scorers with a minimum length or combine them with other evidence.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Verification: accepting a match only when the odds reach a billion
md: The verification math assumes stray detections are independent and uniform. Satellite trails, diffraction spikes (the straight rays that bright stars show because light bends around the supports holding the telescope's secondary mirror), plate scratches and dense clusters violate that, so false positives there are far more common than the formula predicts. Mask streaks before solving.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
md: All three systems are the same idea as lesson 3: name cells with integers, cover the query with cells, read those cells, then refine. S2 and H3 trade geohash's simplicity for cells that behave well everywhere on the sphere, including poles and the antimeridian.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Best fit, splitting and merging inside segments
md: Misconception: "OOM with lots of reserved memory means a leak." Often it is fragmentation: the free memory exists but in holes smaller than the request, inside segments that cannot be released because a live tensor still occupies part of them.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: How a warp's 32 addresses become 32-byte sectors
md: **Misconception:** coalescing requires thread k to read element k. It does not. The Programming Guide notes that permuted access within the same 32-byte segments is just as good. What matters is the ratio of bytes used to bytes transferred.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes
md: Remember the order. The timeline sets the denominator for everything else: a kernel that is 4 percent of the wall time can never give you more than 4 percent, however bad its counters look.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Warps and SIMT: 32 threads, one instruction, and divergence
md: SIMT is not the same as SIMD. In CPU SIMD one instruction works on several values packed into one wide vector register (8 floats in a 256-bit AVX register, for example), and the software sees the vector width and manages lanes itself. In SIMT you write scalar per-thread code and the hardware groups it. Correctness never depends on warps; performance does, much like cache lines.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Community summaries and map-reduce global search
md: Global search is not cheap per query. The docs call it resource-intensive: the map step makes one LLM call per batch of reports, so lower (more detailed) levels cost more calls. Picking the community level is a quality versus cost dial.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Why PPO is costly for LLMs and what GRPO removes
md: GRPO removes the **critic**, not the reward. In DeepSeekMath, GRPO was trained against a learned reward model. Rule-based verifiable rewards came to the fore with DeepSeek-R1. GRPO and RLVR are separate ideas that work well together.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: GTFS Realtime messages and decoding them in Python
md: With FULL_DATASET, each fetch is the entire current state. If a trip's update was in the last message but is missing from this one, the consumer must treat it as having no realtime data now, and the reference is explicit that no TripUpdate does **not** mean the trip is on time.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Kevin Mitnick: social engineering and the longest sentence of its day
md: "We'll train staff not to be fooled" is a weak defence on its own: a skilled caller is persuasive and polite, and the help desk is measured on speed. Build the process so that even a fooled agent cannot complete a reset without the out-of-band check.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: 2010: Operation Aurora and Stuxnet bring state operations into view
md: Aurora showed that a perimeter fails the moment one inside device is compromised, which led to per-request, device-aware access (zero trust). Stuxnet showed that code can break machines and that isolated networks are reached by people carrying media.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: What the incidents changed: laws, institutions and safer defaults
md: Incidents changed security through four channels: law, institutions, defaults and architecture. Defaults and architecture protect people who never read a bulletin, so they matter most. When you meet a new incident, ask the five questions, then ask which of the four channels should change.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Out-of-order and speculative execution, from zero
md: Speculation is safe for *results* and unsafe for *secrets*. The CPU guarantees that mispredicted work never changes what a program computes, but it was never designed to hide that the work happened. Every attack in lessons 7 to 11 is a way to steer transient instructions and then read their footprint.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: CL.TE and TE.CL: two parsers, one stream
md: A desync needs only this: one hop reads **fewer** body bytes than the hop in front of it. The bytes it did not read become the start of the next request on that connection. Reject ambiguous framing at every hop and close the connection whenever framing is in doubt.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Web cache deception: making the cache keep a private page
md: Defence in depth matters here because the origin and the cache are often owned by different teams. The origin team should mark every personalised response `Cache-Control: no-store, private`; the CDN team should make sure no rule overrides that. Either alone has been bypassed in practice.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
md: `enabled=madvise` turns THP into an opt-in: only regions the application marks with `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` get huge pages at fault time. The THP doc recommends it where wasted memory matters, and `madvise(MADV_COLLAPSE)` (Linux 6.1+) lets a program request a synchronous collapse of a range.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
md: Known weak spots from the NVIDIA study: the 16K and 32K hybrids trailed the Transformer by about 1 point on long-context tasks, mostly multi-document QA where distractor passages may confuse the SSM state. Hybrids were also more prompt-sensitive: on MuSiQue the hybrid ranged 10.63 to 16.16 across prompt tweaks vs 15.25 to 17.68 for the Transformer.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Worked toy: how averaging fake answers changes the ranking
md: Averaging fixes errors that differ from sample to sample. It cannot fix an error every sample shares, such as the LLM misunderstanding an ambiguous or unfamiliar query. That is the root of HyDE's main failure mode in lesson 5.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: DNP3, S7comm and OPC UA: from no security to secure by design
md: Secure protocols only help when they are on. An OPC UA server left in mode None, a DNP3 outstation without SAv5 keys, or a Modbus/TCP Security device that also listens on plain port 502 gives the attacker the old, unauthenticated path.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Incident response in OT: safety first, then manual
md: Two IT reflexes can hurt in OT: rebooting or reimaging a running HMI or server (NIST: rebooting 'may not be acceptable'), and running active scans across the control network during an incident. Both can stop the process or the operators' only view of it.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: XML signature wrapping: the verifier and the app read different parts
md: One parse, one element. The code that verifies the signature must hand the verified element to the code that makes decisions, and nothing else in the document may be consulted. Any second search of the document, by name, by position or by a second parser, reopens the gap.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Detecting forged federation tokens and recovering trust
md: Resetting passwords, re-enrolling MFA or rebuilding one server does not remove a forged-token capability. Until the signing key is replaced everywhere it is trusted and the attacker's access is gone, the actor can mint a fresh login whenever they like.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Separation of duties: toxic combinations and two-person control
md: Separation of duties makes misuse require collusion. Write the conflicting pairs down, check requests against them (preventive), scan existing access (detective), and add a mitigating control wherever a split is impossible.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Solving for a homography with the DLT, by hand
md: A homography maps points only after dividing by the third coordinate. Code that multiplies by H and keeps the first two entries silently computes the wrong point everywhere except where W happens to be 1.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: The IR lifecycle: NIST 800-61r3, CSF 2.0 and SANS PICERL
md: Rev. 3's main shift is not new phases but a new framing: IR is part of everyday cybersecurity risk management, and improvement is continuous rather than a meeting at the end.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Memory forensics: processes, connections and injected code
md: Memory answers "what is running right now and talking to whom", which disk forensics cannot. That is why memory is captured first and why rebooting a suspect machine before capture is so costly.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: SQL injection step by step: watching the query change
md: Removing the word OR, or blocking the quote character, is not a fix. It breaks real users (O'Brien, a shop in Portland OR) and misses inputs that need neither, such as a numeric field (lesson 6). The fix is to stop building SQL text out of input.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Submitting, waiting and how the kernel runs a request
md: Completions can arrive in **any order**. The ring preserves the order in which requests are *attempted*, not the order in which they *finish*. Always identify a CQE by its `user_data` (often a pointer to your per-request state), never by its position.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Debug ports: UART, JTAG and SWD, and how makers lock them
md: Do not rely on hiding the pads (no labels, pins removed, epoxy). Those slow a curious owner and stop nobody determined. Treat physical obscurity as a delay, and make the chip itself refuse: burned debug fuses, disabled ROM download modes, no console login.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: One thread for every request: how Node.js runs JavaScript
md: Node.js runs all JavaScript for all users on one Event Loop in one process with the user's full privileges. That gives JavaScript servers two bug classes that matter more than elsewhere: input that blocks the loop (denial of service for everyone) and input that changes shared objects (a change that persists for every later request).

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: child_process: shells, arguments and Windows batch files
md: Prefer `execFile` or `spawn` with an argument array and no shell; put `--` before user-supplied values; validate values against an allowlist of expected forms; never combine an array with `shell: true`; and on Windows treat every batch file call as a shell call.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: mimalloc: three free lists per page
md: mimalloc replaces a per-thread cache with ownership: the thread that owns a page allocates and frees into it with plain loads and stores, and everyone else uses a per-page atomic list that the owner drains in batches.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: The knobs, and how fast the space grows
md: The search space is a product, so it grows exponentially in the number of knobs and linearly in the number of shapes you tune for. Any plan that says "just benchmark them all" has to survive that product.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Handing the device to user space: vfio-pci, BARs and DMA memory
md: No IOMMU, no safety. `uio_pci_generic`, `igb_uio` and VFIO's `enable_unsafe_noiommu_mode` let the device DMA to any physical address. A bug in the application then corrupts the kernel or other processes: the ixy authors report losing a filesystem to rogue DMA writes on a misconfigured server. DPDK recommends vfio-pci with the IOMMU enabled.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: BYOVD: a signed driver with a dangerous interface
md: Misconception: "we only allow signed drivers, so kernel malware is handled." Requiring signatures stops *unsigned* code. BYOVD uses *signed* code that is dangerous by design or by bug. You need a second layer that can refuse specific signed files: the blocklist, App Control deny rules, or the 2026 cross-signed trust removal.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Detection as code for drivers: Sigma rules, tests and conversion
md: Driver detection works best in layers of precision: an exact-match rule (known-bad hashes, CodeIntegrity blocks and revocations) that pages, and an anomaly rule (unusual path, bad signature status, not in inventory) that someone reviews daily.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels
md: Training the student on the teacher's top-1 prediction alone, its single most likely class (pseudo-labeling), is not the same thing in general (lesson 9 shows one setting where top-1 targets did well). It keeps the teacher's decision but discards the relative probabilities of the other classes, which is exactly the extra signal that makes distillation work.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: On-policy distillation in code: student samples, teacher scores
md: For language models, decide two things: what sequences you train on (references, teacher outputs, or the student's own samples) and which divergence you minimize (forward KL covers all modes, reverse KL picks one). On-policy training fixes the train-inference mismatch, and per-token reverse KL turns the teacher into a dense, per-token reward.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
md: Keys: quantize per channel, because outliers live in fixed channels. Values: quantize per token, because the output mixes value rows. Keep the most recent tokens in full precision until a group is complete.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keep everything, read less: query-aware pages and head-aware budgets
md: DuoAttention needs a short optimization per model (several hours on an 8-GPU node, per the paper) and its gates are only as good as the synthetic task; Quest needs a kernel that reads selected pages and computes bounds. Neither is a configuration flag.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Hiding the transfer: layer-wise loading and asynchronous saving
md: Overlap turns load plus compute into roughly max(load, compute). It is free speed when the two are balanced and nearly useless when one dominates.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Vector clocks: detecting concurrency exactly
md: Lamport clocks give one-way causality in one integer. Vector clocks give exact causality and detect concurrency, at the cost of one integer per node in every timestamp and every message.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
md: Late interaction is not free accuracy. You pay in index size, in memory bandwidth at query time, and in engine support. For large text corpora a common design is a cheap first stage (BM25 or a single-vector index) with ColBERT or ColPali scoring a few hundred candidates.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: BFS-like (breadth-first-search-like) is an interpretation from probing, not a built-in algorithm. Coconut was never trained to search, keeps no explicit visited set, and the parallelism narrows after a couple of thoughts.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
md: A learned index does not return approximate answers. It finds exactly the same record a B-tree would. Only the *path* to the record is approximate; the final local search makes the answer exact.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: From MLM logits to one weight per vocabulary term
md: Misconception: the expansion terms are synonyms. They are whatever the MLM head plus ranking training found useful. The paper's own example document about bow legs gains *leg* and *treatment*, but also *arrow* (bow and arrow) and *teeth*, with small weights.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART in practice: libraries, truncation and click bias
md: In production, LambdaMART is the training objective of a tree ensemble that rescores the top candidates of a first-stage retriever. Its quality depends on labels (judgments or debiased clicks), query-grouped data, and a truncation level that matches the positions users see.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: One family, many transitions: RetNet to GLA, Mamba2, RWKV-7, KDA
md: To place a new linear-attention layer, ask two questions. What is $A_t$: identity, scalar, diagonal, identity minus rank 1, or diagonal plus low rank? And what does the write minimize: a dot-product reward (additive) or a regression error (delta)? Richer $A_t$ means finer forgetting and a costlier kernel.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Processes, PIDs, process trees and signals
md: Read processes as a tree. Who started a process (its parent, its user, its command line in `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`) usually tells you more than its name, because names are trivial to fake.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: What an intruder touches: persistence and where defenders look
md: Do not investigate a live compromise only with the compromised system's own tools if you can avoid it: an intruder with root can alter `ps`, `ls` or the logs. Cross-check with package verification, a trusted copy of the tools, or off-host data.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring a service sandbox with systemd-analyze security
md: `systemd-analyze security` turns sandboxing into a number you can track per unit and gate in CI with `--offline=yes --threshold=`. Lower is better, but the score covers only systemd's own settings and cannot tell you what the service legitimately needs.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Falco: turning the system call stream into alerts
md: Falco = driver (modern eBPF by default) + state + YAML rules (condition, output, priority, macros, lists). It detects, it does not block. Every exclusion you add is a deliberate blind spot; write it down.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Patching a fleet: automatic updates, restarts, reboots and rings
md: Automate installation (unattended-upgrades, dnf-automatic), automate restarts (needrestart), schedule reboots or livepatch urgent kernel fixes, roll out in rings with canaries, and verify the running version, not the package database.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
md: For pointwise relevance grades the order bias has an analogue: grading many passages in one prompt lets earlier passages anchor later ones. Grade one passage per call, as the Bing and UMBRELA prompts do, or randomise and repeat if you batch.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Threat model: how an LLM app gets attacked or goes wrong
md: OWASP's top LLM risk guidance says it is unclear whether fool-proof prevention of prompt injection exists, and recommends treating the model as an untrusted user. Design so that a fully hijacked model still cannot do much damage: least-privilege tools (each tool gets only the permissions its job needs), human approval for high-risk actions, and checks outside the model.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size
md: Model weights are paid once; KV is paid per token per sequence. A common mistake is to size a deployment by "the model fits on the GPU". A model that fits with 2 GB to spare can serve almost nobody: 2 GB is only about 15,000 tokens of Llama 3 8B's KV cache.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: How vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM put it together
md: Strip away names and every engine is the same loop: a scheduler spending a per-step token budget, a block allocator answering whether it fits, and a policy for when it does not. The engines differ mainly in that last policy and in how they reuse cached blocks.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Why hard constraints need filters, not similarity
md: The LLM never touches the documents. It only translates the query into a filter object. Exact enforcement is done by the search engine, which is cheap, deterministic and testable.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
md: Calls set the latency floor and the per-call overhead; tokens set the bill. Listwise minimizes calls, not tokens. PRP buys robustness to prompt order with 20 to 100 times more prompts than pointwise (220 to 1,100 times more than listwise) at k = 100.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
md: Both pointwise methods need token log-probabilities. Many chat APIs only return generated text, which is why the RankGPT authors could not run them on GPT-4. And because each passage is scored alone, the score must be comparable across passages (calibrated), which the PRP paper argues LLMs are not trained to provide.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: SIFT: keypoints across scale and a 128-number descriptor
md: A SIFT keypoint carries position, scale and orientation. The descriptor is computed in that local frame, which is why it survives zoom and rotation, and its 128 entries are L2-normalized and clipped for lighting robustness.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Treiber stack: one CAS on the top pointer
md: Pop reads `old->next` after loading `old` but before its CAS. If another thread pops `old` and frees it in that gap, the read touches freed memory. Worse, if the node is reused before the CAS, the CAS can still succeed with a stale `next`. That is the ABA problem, and it is the subject of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drain: a fixed-depth parse tree and a similarity threshold
md: The one thing to remember: Drain bounds the work per line to a fixed tree walk plus a comparison against the few groups in one leaf, which makes its cost $O(n)$ in the number of lines. It buys that speed with two assumptions, that same-template lines share a token count and that early tokens are constants.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Normalisation: one event, one shape (ECS and OCSF)
md: A Windows 4625 converted to ECS and an sshd failure converted to ECS look identical to a rule, which is the point, but also a risk: a mapping mistake (say, putting the target host into source.ip) now breaks every rule at once. Test mappings with sample events from each source, exactly like rules (lesson 11).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Baselines, anomalies and UEBA: how Storm-0558 was caught
md: State's advantage was not a product; it was three years of studying normal mailbox access, which let a modest-looking event stand out. The CSRB notes that buying the logs alone would not have been enough: few organisations analysed that voluminous log in detail.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Other routes to long context: base scaling, searched factors, data
md: Long data alone was not enough. Xiong et al. report that with Llama 2's original base the model still could not attend effectively beyond about 4,000 to 6,000 tokens after extensive long-context continual pretraining. Changing the base of a finished model without training, on the other hand, is just NTK-aware scaling with a huge s. The knob and the training go together.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Does the model use its context? Evaluation
md: Extending RoPE (PI, NTK, YaRN) makes long positions *in distribution*; Ring Attention and context parallelism make long sequences *fit*; neither guarantees the model *uses* the context. Measure effective length with depth-controlled tasks such as RULER.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Build it: loop your GPT with input injection and random depth
md: Everything here is one seed of a 219K-parameter model on a synthetic task. Treat the numbers as a demonstration of the mechanism (more iterations resolve deeper chains, exits track depth, starts are forgotten), not as evidence about which adapter is better at scale.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
md: LoRA = frozen W0 + (alpha/r) B A, with B initialized to zero. You train r times (d + k) numbers per adapted matrix, and the model starts exactly at the pretrained one.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: Exact unlearning means the result is what retraining without the forget set would give. SISA keeps that guarantee by confining each point's influence to one shard and one suffix of slices, so only that part is retrained.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
md: Low scores on forget benchmarks show suppressed outputs, not erased knowledge. Small fine-tunes, probes and even 4-bit quantization can bring "forgotten" knowledge back, because approximate unlearning moves the weights only slightly.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Notarization, revocation and the Shlayer lesson
md: Notarization means "Apple's automated scan found nothing known-bad when this was uploaded". It is not a review of intent, and it can be fooled by code that only turns malicious later or hides its payload. Its real strength is speed of revocation once something is reported.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Case: Atomic Stealer and the paste-into-Terminal era
md: Resetting the user's password is not enough after a stealer. Session cookies stolen from the browser let the attacker into SaaS apps without the password or MFA until those sessions are revoked server-side.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The PE format: headers, sections and what imports reveal
